profile.site: Former Regions Lakeshore Operations Center plus adjoining parcels at 250 and 260 Milan Parkway and 2500 Venice Road, approximately 75 to 80 acres, acquired for about 90 million dollars in transactions closing 2025-09-30 through affiliate Alabama ADC Holdings LLC
profile.phases: Two phases; second 200 MW phase targeted fall 2028
profile.address: 201 Milan Parkway, Oxmoor Corporate Park, Birmingham, AL 35211
profile.reading: Nebius Group is a publicly traded, Nasdaq-listed AI cloud infrastructure company under ticker NBIS, spun out from Yandex in 2024 after Yandex sold its Russian domestic business and retained its international operations under the Nebius name, headquartered in Amsterdam. The company provides GPU infrastructure access for AI workloads to major customers including Microsoft and Meta, and operates or leases data center capacity across Finland, the UK, France, Israel, Iceland, and multiple US locations, with a stated target of 2.5 gigawatts of contracted capacity by the end of 2026. In Alabama, Nebius is developing a project called BHM01 on roughly 80 acres in Birminghams Oxmoor area, targeting as much as 300 megawatts of capacity according to online reporting, though full details of the projects scope remained unclear as of the research date. A Nebius affiliate, Alabama ADC Holdings LLC, purchased four properties in 2025 for a combined 90 million dollars from the University of Alabama at Birmingham, Regions Bank, and U.S. Steel, including the former Regions Lakeshore Operations Center at 201 Milan Parkway, which is planned for demolition and replacement with new facilities, with an affiliate of real estate firm Raeden also acquiring nearby properties in the same area. The Birmingham project faces local headwinds, as the city was, as of the research date, considering a moratorium on new data center development in response to community opposition tied to other regional projects, a dynamic that could affect the ultimate scale and timeline of Nebiuss Alabama buildout. This research was carried out at the operator level in an earlier phase of this project.
profile.regulatory: Birmingham city attorney determined in April 2026 that the switching station and substation did not require city approval; a residents class action filed 2026-05-13 and amended 2026-05-25 names Nebius, Hoar Construction, the City of Birmingham, Raeden LLC and affiliates
profile.source_note: No Nebius press release for Birmingham was located on 2026-09-01; the 300 MW figure is reported by DCD, WBHM and BirminghamWatch citing city proceedings, not published by the operator. Treat as planned capacity from secondary sources until Nebius files or announces it.

reading.body:
Nebius is building a 300 MW AI data center on 75 to 80 acres in Birmingham, Alabama, acquired for approximately 90 million dollars, with first-phase construction underway and full build-out targeted for 2028.

The facility represents a significant AI compute investment in a region without prior data center infrastructure at this scale. The project consolidates a former banking operations center with adjoining land, suggesting that repurposed industrial real estate can serve AI's power and thermal demands when paired with utility capacity. Alabama Power provides the electricity. The two-phase timeline, with a second 200 MW phase targeting fall 2028, indicates the developer's confidence in sustained demand beyond the first phase.

The project faced regulatory friction uncommon in data center development. Birmingham had a data center moratorium in place when the facility was planned. The city attorney determined in April 2026 that switching and substation equipment did not require city approval, effectively circumventing the moratorium. A resident class action filed in May 2026 names the city, the operator, and construction firm as defendants. This conflict between local governance and data center growth is not itself a compute constraint, but it signals the political friction that infrastructure expansion now encounters in population centers.

The 300 MW figure comes from secondary sources citing city proceedings, not from Nebius announcements. This is worth noting because it reflects how AI infrastructure planning now happens partly outside traditional corporate disclosure. The facility is modelled on Nebius's 75 MW Mantsala plant in Finland, indicating operational precedent but no published performance data specific to this site or operator.
